items.title: Only 9% of major companies use biodiversity indicators, study finds
items.desc: Biodiversity indicators can help companies make more sustainable decisions. But only 9% of the world's largest companies in sectors with a major impact on biodiversity use such indicators, according to a new study from Lund University. The researchers also show that different indicators can lead to different conclusions and present seven recommendations for how they should be used.

items.title: The genetic switch behind the butterfly's enhanced visual world of color
items.desc: Many insects see the world through hundreds of tiny lenses that are grouped together in a visual organ known as the compound eye. Behind each lens sits a cluster of eight light-detecting cells arranged in a pattern that scientists believe has existed for hundreds of millions of years.

items.title: Cows deliver healthy calves without embryonic protein long thought essential for pregnancy
items.desc: For decades, scientists have believed that a protein called interferon tau (IFNT) is indispensable for pregnancy in cattle. Produced by the early embryo, it was thought to signal its presence to the mother and prevent the hormonal changes that would otherwise end the pregnancy.

items.title: Stratospheric winds can warn of extreme energy demand in Europe
items.desc: A breakdown of normal polar winds in winter raises the chance of extreme cold—and a resulting spike in energy demand—in Europe, new research shows. Normally, strong and stable westerly winds circle high above the Arctic in the winter, in what is known as the "stratospheric polar vortex."

items.title: Chance Instagram sighting leads to discovery of rare giant water lily in Colombia
items.desc: A new paper published in the journal Phytotaxa describes a new species in the genus Victoria, the Colombian giant water lily (Victoria colombiana). With only three other known species in the genus, V. colombiana joins the pantheon of nature's giants with pads measuring up to 2 meters (6.6 feet) across.

items.title: Bees struggle to smell flowers when air pollutants combine
items.desc: Bees, moths and other pollinating insects have a harder time smelling flowers in polluted air, according to research led by the University of Reading. Scientists analyzed 22 experimental studies on how the air pollutants ozone and nitrogen oxides (NOx) affect pollinators. Both pollutants make it harder for pollinators to find flowers by breaking down or altering the scents that flowers give off.

items.title: Netherlands report maps ecological and social aspects of large-scale carbon removal
items.desc: There is a strong national and international commitment to large-scale carbon removal from the atmosphere (Carbon Dioxide Removal, CDR) to achieve climate goals. But how do you do that responsibly? A study commissioned by the Climate Research Initiative Netherlands (KIN) and led by the University of Twente shows which ecological and social effects and preconditions must be taken into account.

items.title: Sentinel-3C returns its first views of Earth
items.desc: Just two weeks after it was launched, the Copernicus Sentinel-3C satellite returned its first images and measurements from two of its key instruments—a major milestone that confirms the satellite is working well and on track to monitor the health of Earth's oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere.

items.title: Informal food vendors: The invisible backbone of the world's food system
items.desc: Walk through almost any city or town in a low-income or middle-income country and you'll pass them: the woman selling deep-fried fish from a cart, the mobile vendor with a bicycle full of vegetables, the kiosk operator who's the only source of a hot meal within walking distance. Food systems employ an estimated 1.23 billion people globally, and a majority of those jobs are informal—unlicensed, unregistered or otherwise outside the reach of formal regulation. items.title: Fossil bite marks suggest first evidence of a small raptor feeding on an apex predator
items.desc: A prehistoric cold case near Drumheller reveals either a small-time raptor scavenged on an apex predator, or a baby Albertosaurus engaged in a shocking act of cannibalism. These two possible explanations for what happened to an Albertosaurus after its death near Drumheller are wildly divergent.

items.title: New framework links digital technology and mineral processing to support Africa's economic growth
items.desc: Research published in the International Journal of Business Innovation and Research (IJBIR) suggests that African economies need to move beyond fragmented development strategies. This might be done by uniting digital technology, startup networks, resource processing and cross-sector partnerships into a single societal innovation ecosystem, the researchers explain.

items.title: New 'computational microscope' simulates DNA packaging at more than ten times previous scale
items.desc: The DNA in our cells wraps around proteins called histones to form nucleosomes, which organize into chromatin. This organization helps pack genetic material into the nucleus and influences how easily genes can be read and DNA damage repaired. Understanding how chromatin changes requires studying molecular movements and interactions that are difficult to capture experimentally.

items.title: Chemists uncover the true active surface of nickel catalysts
items.desc: Nickel is a promising, cost-effective and robust catalyst for alkaline water electrolysis—a key technology for the climate-neutral production of hydrogen. However, the actual structure of the active surface of such nickel electrodes under reaction conditions had not yet been conclusively determined. A research team at Ulm University has now refuted a decades-old assumption: The catalytically active surface does not consist of nickel oxyhydroxide (NiOOH), as was previously widely assumed, but is nickel dioxide (NiO₂). The findings have been published in the journal Nature Catalysis.

items.title: Bavaria's ancestral languages: Resisting linguistic genocide
items.desc: My ancestral languages, Boarisch (Bavarian) and Schwäbisch (Swabian), are routinely described as German dialects. That might sound like a technical linguistic distinction. For me, a Boarisch-Schwob scholar and community member, it raises a practical question: What happens to a people when their ancestral language, which carries their identity and "Weltanschauung" (worldview), is excluded from protection under a European language treaty because the modern state and dominant culture reduce it to a dialect?

items.title: Lensless imaging method enables long-term monitoring of living cells without staining
items.desc: In a study led by Tampere University, researchers have developed a new lensless imaging method that produces precise quantitative data on living cells from a single image. The compact system can be placed inside a standard cell-culture incubator, allowing living cells to be monitored continuously for hours or even days without staining or other labels. The research is published in the journal Applied Physics Letters.

items.title: NASA is searching for hidden caves to build its first Moon base
items.desc: NASA is preparing for humanity’s first Moon base with three investigations that will hunt for underground shelters, uncover hidden ice, and track dangerous conditions on the lunar surface. The findings could reveal how astronauts can survive and thrive on the Moon while laying the groundwork for future journeys to Mars.

items.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
items.desc: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

items.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
items.desc: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

items.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
items.desc: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

items.title: NASA’s Webb finds signs of Mars-sized worlds smashing together
items.desc: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope is giving astronomers a glimpse of the kinds of violent collisions that may have shaped our own solar system, including the giant impact thought to have created the Moon. By studying 21 rare “extreme debris disks” around young stars, researchers found that their dust can reveal the scale and intensity of planetary collisions.

items.title: FDA-approved epilepsy drug may help reverse osteoarthritis damage
items.desc: Researchers at Yale have identified a promising new approach to osteoarthritis that could do more than simply ease pain. The epilepsy drug lacosamide appears to block a protein involved in both pain signaling and cartilage destruction, helping damaged joints shift back toward repair in preclinical studies.

items.title: Einstein Probe reveals a hidden phase of neutron star collisions
items.desc: Einstein Probe revealed nearly 10 minutes of soft X-ray activity following a short gamma-ray burst, exposing a phase of neutron star mergers that previous missions may have missed. The prolonged emission could have been powered by a newly formed magnetar and may provide a valuable new counterpart to gravitational-wave signals.

items.title: Just 7 days of strength training started shrinking fat cells in mice
items.desc: Just seven strength-training sessions helped obese mice shrink visceral fat cells and reactivate molecular pathways involved in burning stored fat, despite no change in overall body weight. The findings suggest some benefits of resistance exercise may begin long before weight loss becomes visible, though the results still need to be confirmed in humans.

items.title: Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
items.desc: Giving zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule appears to bring out more natural behavior. The lions spent nearly three times longer feeding, engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food, and rested more heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.

items.title: Stanford scientists turn a cancer driver into a kill switch
items.desc: A Stanford-designed molecule turns a major lymphoma-promoting protein against cancer cells, activating their own self-destruct machinery instead of simply blocking tumor growth. In mice, the treatment completely eliminated aggressive human lymphoma tumors within 11 days, although much more testing is needed before it could reach patients.

items.title: Humans may not be as hardwired for violence as we thought
items.desc: A study comparing 100 primate species, including humans, suggests that everyday aggression and lethal violence did not evolve as part of the same simple behavioral spectrum. Species that frequently fight or show mild aggression are not necessarily more likely to kill rivals, while extreme acts such as infanticide and lethal attacks appear to follow their own evolutionary patterns.

items.title: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
items.desc: The James Webb Space Telescope has found strong evidence that the rocky lava world HD 3167 b has an atmosphere, despite circling its star every 24 hours under extreme heat. The surprising discovery could help scientists understand how rocky planets retain atmospheres and what the young, molten Earth may once have looked like.

items.title: Don't miss: Watch Saturn shine and Halley’s Comet debris streak across the sky
items.desc: October skywatchers can see Saturn at opposition, catch meteors from Halley’s Comet during the Orionid peak, and watch the Moon sweep past the famous Pleiades star cluster. Moonlight may obscure some Orionids, but the best viewing should come before dawn after the Moon sets.

items.title: Earth’s center is moving, and NASA just measured it
items.desc: Earth’s center of mass is constantly on the move, shifting by a few millimeters as enormous amounts of water, ice, and even air migrate around the planet with the seasons. NASA scientists have developed a more precise way to track these tiny swings using laser-ranging satellites, GPS data, and measurements of how water and ice deform Earth’s crust.

items.title: Physicists just found the ‘ghost’ of superconductivity
items.desc: Physicists have found striking evidence for an unusual form of superconducting behavior in uranium ditelluride, where electron pairs organize into rippling patterns called pair density waves. Even more surprisingly, these patterns appear to survive after ordinary superconductivity disappears, suggesting that the electron pairs responsible for superconductivity may begin forming before the material actually becomes superconducting.

items.title: MAGA’s Self-Destructive Culture War
items.desc: Polls suggest that MAGA fanaticism might not be playing so well outside US President Donald Trump’s loyal base. But if the Democrats want to retake one or both chambers of Congress, they should concentrate on the economy and not answer Republican extremism with a culture war of their own.

items.title: How to Break the German Malaise
items.desc: For too long, Germany’s political and corporate elite coasted on the country’s postwar economic and political success story, avoiding difficult but necessary reforms that could have kept extremist populist parties at bay. Now that the barbarians are at the gates, mainstream elites must rethink everything.

items.title: Europe’s Place in the Global Redivision of Labor
items.desc: While the US continues to lead in software, some high-tech sectors, and hydrocarbons, China is becoming increasingly competitive in many high-tech, capital-intensive sectors, not least those once dominated by Europe. The EU does have a relative advantage in this new economic order, if only its leaders would recognize it.

items.title: The World Has Passed Peak Trump
items.desc: US President Donald Trump, previously the most powerful, unpredictable force on the international stage, has now passed the peak of his ability to disrupt the international order. With his approval ratings collapsing, foreign leaders whose tenures will extend beyond his own are starting to write him off.

items.title: Global Financial Reform that Centers African Women
items.desc: While gender-equality objectives often fall by the wayside in times of upheaval, the current rupture in the multilateral order creates an opportunity to build a debt architecture that will deliver for the women of Africa. The first steps toward this goal can be taken at this month’s IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.

items.title: How Africa Can Leverage the US-China Thaw
items.desc: As dollar borrowing costs soar, Chinese rates are approaching record lows. This divergence, combined with the US-China thaw, creates an opportunity for African governments: partner with the US on gas and with China on solar and storage, and tap lower-cost Asian capital markets to finance investments in both.

items.title: Closing NATO’s Deterrence Gap
items.desc: With Russian provocations against NATO member states growing more frequent, the alliance urgently needs to develop a credible doctrine of punitive deterrence to guide its response to acts of aggression that fall below the threshold of war. Mere territorial defense is not enough.

items.title: The India-Pakistan Cold War
items.desc: The current stalemate between India and Pakistan should be viewed not as a pause between rounds of negotiation, but rather as part of a deliberate Indian strategy of disengagement. India will return to the negotiating table only after Pakistan dismantles, comprehensively and verifiably, its state-supported terrorist networks.

items.title: The Next Era of Reform Must Be About Capability
items.desc: Economic development should no longer be measured solely by how much finance is mobilized or how much fiscal space is created. It must also be judged by whether countries emerge more capable of setting their own priorities, responding to challenges, and seizing new opportunities to shape their own future.

items.title: With AI, Sharing Is Caring
items.desc: Although the public's distrust of Big Tech is understandable, given past experience, that is not a reason to starve AI models of the information and data they will need to be useful. If serving the public interest is the goal, everyone relying on the technology's output has a duty to provide high-quality input.

items.title: Why the US-China Trade Truce Matters
items.desc: Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump’s agreement to extend their trade truce reflects the fact that both sides have leverage over the other. In a world where the rules-based trading system is not functioning, the current fragile equilibrium may be the best one can hope for.

items.title: Brazil’s Voters Have Moved
items.desc: A strong performance by the right-wing, Donald Trump-aligned candidate in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election demonstrates that the left-wing ruling party has failed to keep up with the times. The Brazilian electorate is older, more devout, and more preoccupied with crime and personal security than it once was.

items.title: Does Inclusive Finance Really Need Stablecoins?
items.desc: Today, 1.3 billion adults—more than half of them women—remain excluded from the formal financial system, and lower-income consumers still struggle to find and access the financial products and services they need. Contrary to much hype, stablecoins are not the best way to solve either of these problems.

items.desc: Brazil's left has just suffered a crushing election defeat and will most likely lose the presidency at the end of October. The causes are many, beginning with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's longstanding refusal to groom an appealing successor.
